chapter_theme: The king, having followed his queen in the night and seen her with a base lover, spares them in thought and turns from desire; after a hard day of pretence in court he goes to his mother, who tells him to kill a kid to the goddess against his dream, and he refuses to take one life to save his own.

cast.role: the king, husband of the unfaithful queen; unnamed in this chapter
the king's queen, who goes to a low man at night
the low man the queen visits, unnamed
the king's mother, named at verse 132
the goddess to whom the mother tells him to offer a kid

118.reading: The king rises from sleep, takes up his bright sword and, like a lion pacing in madness, steals after the fish-eyed queen, hiding so as to learn what she will do.
118.nuance: The queen is not named in the verse; she is 'she of the fish-like eyes'. The sword in his hand is what verse 123 turns back.
118.event: The king leaves his bed with sword in hand and secretly follows the queen to see her conduct.

119.reading: The low man seizes the lotus-like woman by her dark hair, drags her over the ground, strikes her with both hands and throws her down, demanding that she say what kept her late.
119.nuance: The man is called கடையன், 'the lowest', and is not named; that he is her lover is read from the sequel in verses 120 to 122. The king's own contempt for such a man comes at verse 124.
119.event: The low man beats and tramples the queen, demanding to know why she was delayed.

120.reading: The woman lies choked and silent like the moon swallowed by darkness; when he sees her stir only a little, the bewildered man in his confusion puts her flower-soft feet on his head.
120.nuance: The same man who struck her now worships her feet: the verse shows the rule of desire, in which the beater is the servant.
120.event: The man, seeing her faint after his blows, grovels and sets her feet on his head.

121.reading: Recovering slowly, the woman looks gladly at the man and tells him not to be angry: she sat beside the king on the throne in the royal hall, she says, and speaks of cruel sins and a ripening she will not name.
121.nuance: Lines 3 and 4 are hard: 'cruel sins' (வெய்ய பாவங்கள்) may refer to what she did with the king or to her own wrong, and 'what ripened' is left unsaid. The reading is provisional.
121.event: The queen pacifies her lover and excuses her lateness by her place beside the king.

122.reading: She tells him that a wish-granting tree, once seen, is not let go, that her whole love is for him, and asks whether any other companion could stand with him here.
122.nuance: The oath of love is one a wife should keep for her husband; the poem puts it in the mouth of an unfaithful queen, to be heard by the king (verse 123). The image of the wish-granting tree is hers for the low man, and is not the poet's praise of him.
122.event: The queen declares her love to the man while the king overhears.

123.reading: Hearing her, the king's eyes blaze and he resolves to send both to the sword's death; but understanding rises in him and, with the sword in his hand, he stands between his anger and the deed.
123.nuance: The verse says the knowledge came to him as discernment, not as fear or lack of power: the sword is in his hand when he holds back.
123.event: The king, enraged, resolves to kill them, then checks himself on reflection.

124.reading: The king reasons that women, whoever they are, are not fit to be killed, that this fool is like a woman, and that destroying a small, mean birth with the sword made for the heads of kings is not a proper thing.
124.nuance: His two reasons are rank and sex, not mercy: a woman is spared as a woman and the man because he is beneath the sword. The epic gives the king's reason as his own and does not say it is the Jain rule of non-killing; that appears only in verse 139. The unnamed 'low birth' (சிறுபுன் சாதி) is the king's contempt.
124.event: The king decides to spare the woman and her lover.

claims.claim: a woman is not to be put to death, whatever her fault
a king's sword is too high for a small and base person

125.reading: Thinking over all this with scorn, the king puts the pleasures of the women aside, goes back and lies on his scented bed, brooding like a solitary elephant.
125.nuance: Turning from the pleasures of the women (போகம் புறக்கணித்திட்டு) is the first step of his renunciation, named in verse 132.
125.event: The king returns to his bed, gives up the pleasures of the women's quarters and broods.

126.reading: He thinks that desire is the lowest thing: it ruins the mind, destroys the hundred fruits of a high birth, kills fame on earth, feeds blame, breaks the firmness of honour and the strength of manhood, and fades the sight.
126.nuance: The king blames desire and not the woman; it is the same turn he makes in verse 128. His list of what desire destroys ends with the eyes.
126.event: The king concludes that desire is the root of his ruin.

claims.claim: desire destroys thought, fame, honour and manhood and brings blame

127.reading: Even if one speaks of form and beauty and a family of light, he thinks, a woman like Lakshmi herself may be ruined and serve a base man like a worm in filth; to leave off the work of the god of love is best.
127.nuance: Madana (the god of love) is called the one without sense; leaving desire is stated as an excellence (சிறப்பு), and not yet as release.
127.event: The king resolves that giving up desire is the best course.

claims.claim: beauty and high birth are no safeguard against desire's ruin
to leave the doings of desire is the best course

128.reading: The earth-woman, he says, does not belong to those who hold her, and women by nature come together with the meritorious and part again; the right deed is to go beyond them.
128.nuance: The generalisation about women is the king's, made in grief; the poem puts it in his mind and does not say it is its own doctrine. The word for 'deed' (கருமம்) is the duty he takes up in 132.
128.event: The king concludes that passing beyond women and desire is his duty.

claims.claim: a woman's nature is to join whoever merit brings and to leave again
it is right to pass beyond them

129.reading: Next day the king, as before, sits in his place of counsel, hiding what he knows, surrounded by kin who are pleasure to him; the queen comes in due order and sits quietly beside him.
129.nuance: He keeps the secret (மறை புலப்படாமை) so that his own conduct is unchanged; the contrast with the night before is the point of the scene.
129.event: The king keeps his secret and sits in court; the queen takes her usual place by him.

130.reading: As they play, the king flicks a blue lotus from his finger at her and she, with feigned swoon, lets her body drop; she is revived by scented water and comes round.
130.nuance: 'With falsehood' (பொய்யினால்) marks her swoon as put on; the king's play is a test or a jest, and he lets the pretence run, as verse 131 shows.
130.event: The king flicks a flower at the queen and she pretends to swoon.

131.reading: The king, as though in jest, says that the flower, full of holes through which water drips, has almost taken her life, and sends her away with cunning, sighing hard to himself.
131.nuance: His words are a jest in her own pretence: he mocks the fainting and keeps his knowledge from her.
131.event: The king mocks her fainting with a jest and dismisses her, hiding his grief.

132.reading: Intending to give up the kingdom, the king goes to his mother's shrine and bows before Chandramathi; she wishes that he live long beneath his great umbrella as lord of the sea-ringed world.
132.nuance: The mother's blessing is ironic beside the king's purpose: she wishes the opposite of what he has come to say.
132.event: The king, resolved to leave his throne, goes to his mother and bows; she blesses him with long rule.

133.reading: Seeing his gem-bright body faded and his face drooping, she asks why, king of kings, his beauty has gone, whether illness gives her heart great pain, and tells him not to hide it but say.
133.nuance: Her fear is of illness; the cause she will hear is a dream, not a body ailment.
133.event: The mother asks her son why his beauty is gone.

134.reading: The king answers that what the queen saw in the night in a dream, like the bright moon in the sky dimmed and gone into a shadowed darkness, is what eats at his mind.
134.nuance: The verse says the queen saw it (இறைவி ... கனவினிற் கண்டது), and the king's own mind is troubled by it. Whether the dream is the king's or the queen's, in a tale that began with her unfaithfulness, is not settled here.
134.event: The king tells his mother of a dream in the night.

135.reading: The mother tells him not to fear the night's dream as a cause of evil: if he bows to the goddess and honours her, the evil will be dispelled without growing.
135.nuance: This is the mother's view of the dream as an omen. The poem does not answer it directly; it answers the offering that she goes on to name (136 to 139).
135.event: The mother tells the king that worship of the goddess will remove the dream's evil.

claims.claim: worship of the goddess dissolves the evil that a bad dream foretells

136.reading: She names the day, the Tuesday in the bright part of Aippasi after the eighth, and says that if he offers a blood-offering at the goddess's feet, she will accept the living offering and be pleased.
136.nuance: The claim is answered in verse 139 and in the king's shock at 138 (see those verses). The sacrificial goddess is not tied to any named school here.
136.event: The mother names the day and the offering that will please the goddess.

claims.claim: a life offered to the goddess pleases her and averts evil

137.reading: She tells him to cut down a young kid with his victorious sword and give a proper offering to please Chandikai, so the goddess will keep off what his dream showed.
137.nuance: The king's reply at 138-139 refuses the killing, which is the poem's answer; the goddess is named only here.
137.event: The mother tells the king to kill a kid for Chandikai.

claims.claim: killing a kid before Chandikai wards off the dream's evil

138.reading: Without the goddess's grace anywhere in these words, the king, as soon as she speaks, puts his hands to his ears, asks what grace this is, a strange thing, and speaks gently and tenderly to his mother.
138.nuance: The verse says there is no grace (அருளொன்றின்றி) in what she said; that judgment is the narrator's, and it prepares the king's refusal.
138.event: The king covers his ears at his mother's command and begins his reply.

139.reading: The king says that even if his own life were lost he would not plan the good of one life by the end of another; to put an end to a life as a shield for his own, he asks, how can the world be protected, and are kings not the shield of all living creatures?
139.nuance: The king's answer both rejects the offering and gives the reason in the king's own terms (the shield of lives), before anything of doctrine. The sentence is hard to parse in lines 2-3; the reading is provisional.
139.event: The king refuses to kill an animal to save himself.

claims.claim: a king is the guard of living creatures and may not take one life to guard his own
one must not harm a life to protect one's own

links.note: The man who is her chosen lover beats her to the ground; the husband she betrayed holds the sword and refuses to strike.
links.teaches: The two scenes set the lover's blows beside the husband's restraint, so the reader sees whose hand the woman was safer in.

links.note: The king takes up the sword to follow her and, at the climax of his anger, his hand is stopped.
links.teaches: Carrying the sword in verse 118 makes the check in 123 a choice taken with the means to kill in hand, not a failure of means.

links.note: The king has the power to strike and the cause, and holds his anger.
links.teaches: The couplet separates guarding anger where it can take effect from guarding it where it cannot; the king's stand is the first kind, with a sword drawn.

gains.a: The story shows anger held when the means to act are in hand, which is the couplet's hard case.
gains.b: The couplet gets a king for whom guarding anger is a stayed sword, not a mood.

links.note: The king spares the woman and the man, but for reasons of sex and rank, not because life is dear.
links.teaches: The couplet bars killing even to save one's own life without exception; the king's reasons here are narrower, and only at 139 does he come to the couplet's rule.

gains.a: The story shows how an unprincipled restraint falls short of the rule it is made to meet.
gains.b: The couplet's absolute rule is tested against a husband's provoked rage, which it does not itself mention.

links.note: The king lists what desire destroys; the couplet says pain ends when desire, anger and confusion lose even their names.
links.teaches: The couplet states the cure; the king's list shows what it costs when desire is not removed, and he begins the cure by leaving the court.

gains.a: The king's list of damage remains a mood until a doctrine says desire can be removed.
gains.b: The couplet gets a concrete account of what the removed desire costs a man who was ruled by it.

links.note: The Siddhar blames a deceiving demon in woman's form; the king blames desire itself and has just spared the woman.
links.teaches: The Siddhar locates the theft of understanding in the woman, while the king locates it in desire, and so he can leave her alive.

gains.a: The king lacks the Siddhar's picture of desire as a demon that robs understanding.
gains.b: The Siddhar's blame of the woman lacks the king's separation of the woman from her desire.

links.note: The king takes the nature of women as a reason to leave; the quatrain says no guard will keep them from fault.
links.teaches: The quatrain says guards cannot hold women's conduct; the king's answer is not a stronger guard but his own departure.

gains.a: The king's remark on women's nature is given as a general rule that others also hold.
gains.b: The quatrain's counsel of guarding gets a different answer from a husband who has seen guarding fail.

links.note: The king's disenchantment with the court and the queen leads him to leave the throne; the Siddhar lists town, kin, women, glory and wealth as things that do not last.
links.teaches: The Siddhar states what does not last; the king shows the grief and betrayal through which a man comes to accept it.

gains.a: The king's resolve gets a doctrine of impermanence that makes it more than hurt pride.
gains.b: The Siddhar's list gets a worked case in which the loss of a wife and rank is lived, not recited.

links.note: The mother tells him to kill a kid to protect himself; his answer is that no life may be taken to guard his own.
links.teaches: The mother and the son give opposite answers to one fear, and the poem lets the son's answer stand.

links.note: A mother asks for one killing as an offering to a goddess; the couplet says not killing beats a thousand offerings.
links.teaches: The couplet compares not killing with great offerings, while the story puts the offering on a mother's lips as a cure for her son's fear.

gains.a: The story shows the offering asked at a moment of personal fear, which the couplet's comparison lacks.
gains.b: The couplet gives the king's refusal a ground in a rule above the king's own reasoning.

links.note: The mother asks a kid for Chandikai; the Tirumanthiram describes Chandika as holding the four directions, without an offering.
links.teaches: The Tirumanthiram gives Chandika a cosmic form and no offering, while the epic shows how a mother worships her.

gains.a: The epic shows the offering practice and not her cosmic form.
gains.b: The Tirumanthiram's Chandika gets the folk offering that the epic makes the king refuse.

links.note: The poet said he would teach release through leaving cruel deeds; the king's refusal is the first such act in this story.
links.teaches: The opening promise of the poem is enacted in the first refusal of killing, long before any release.

new_concepts.gloss: an offering, especially of a life, made to a deity
new_concepts.label_source: verses 136 and 137 use the word பலி

source_issues: Verse 131 line 3 has a stray '!' after 'என்றென்' in the edition.
Verse 132 line 1 had a doubled vowel sign, repaired by the build.
Verse 135 ends in a comma and verse 136 has no closing mark; the verse boundary is the edition's.
Verses 130 to 131 and 134 are partly obscure; speaker and subject are inferred from the story so far.
